t.5.66.2: In this way, in many different ways, Rāma Dāśarathi should be addressed by you, so that he may quickly win me back after slaying Rāvaṇa in battle.
t.5.66.1: Then, O tiger among men, out of her love for you and out of affection, the queen showed me respect, and I was addressed by her once more with a reply, spoken with great agitation.
t.5.66.3: Or, if you think it fit, O hero, O subduer of foes, stay for a single day in some sheltered place, and, having rested, you shall go tomorrow.
t.5.66.4: And through your presence, O monkey, there may be for a moment, even for me, ill-fated as I am, a release from this bitter fruit of sorrow.
t.5.66.5: For when you, the valiant one, have gone, my very life would hang in doubt until you come back again; of this there is no doubt.
t.5.66.6: The grief born of not seeing you would torment me yet again, sorrow upon sorrow, me who am already overwhelmed by sorrow, wretched, and a partaker of misery.
t.5.66.7: But this very great doubt concerning the heroes, the monkeys and bears who are your allies, stands as it were before me, beyond question.
t.5.66.8: How indeed will those armies of monkeys and bears, or those two sons of the best of men, cross the great ocean so hard to cross?
t.5.66.9: Only three beings have the power to leap across this ocean: Vainateya, Vāyu, or you, O sinless one.
t.5.66.11: Indeed, you alone are fully capable of accomplishing this task, O slayer of enemy heroes; the rise of your might brings you glory.
t.5.66.10: So, O hero, in this charge of duty that is so hard to accomplish, what solution do you see? Tell me, O best among those who know how to accomplish a task.
t.5.66.12: If Rāma, with his entire forces, were to slay Rāvaṇa in battle and, victorious, lead me to his own city, that would bring him glory.
t.5.66.13: Just as I was carried off from the forest through deceit by the rākṣasa, out of fear of that hero, Rāghava ought not to act in the same way.
t.5.66.14: But if Kākutstha, the crusher of enemy forces, were to fill Laṅkā with his armies and then lead me away, that would be worthy of him.
t.5.66.15: So bring it about in such a way that the valor of that great-souled one, a hero in battle, proves worthy of him.
t.5.66.17: O lady, Sugrīva, lord of the armies of monkeys and bears, foremost among leapers and endowed with courage, has firmly resolved to act for your sake.
t.5.66.16: Having heard that speech, rich in meaning, modest and grounded in reason, I then spoke the remaining words in reply.
t.5.66.18: Under his command stand monkeys endowed with valor, full of courage and of great strength, who move as swiftly as the will of the mind.
t.5.66.19: Those of boundless energy, whose course is not obstructed above, nor below, nor sideways, do not falter even in mighty deeds.
t.5.66.20: Again and again the earth has been circumambulated by those illustrious, mighty vānaras, who follow the path of the wind.
t.5.66.21: There are forest-dwellers there who surpass me and others who are my equals; in Sugrīva's presence there is no one inferior to me.
t.5.66.23: Therefore enough of this anguish, O queen; let your grief depart. In a single leap those leaders of the monkey hosts will come to Laṅkā.
t.5.66.22: Even I, such as I am, have reached this place; how much more, then, those mighty ones! For the foremost are not the ones sent; it is the lesser folk who are sent.
t.5.66.24: And those two lions among men, mounted on my back like the risen moon and sun, will come into your presence, O noble lady.
t.5.66.25: Soon you will see Rāghava, the slayer of foes, resembling a lion, and Lakṣmaṇa, bow in hand, arrived at the gate of Laṅkā.
t.5.66.26: Soon you will see the monkeys gathered together, heroes whose weapons are their claws and teeth, with the valour of lions and tigers, resembling the lord of the monkeys himself.
t.5.66.27: Before long you will hear the roar of the foremost of the monkeys, resembling mountains and clouds, as they bellow on the slopes of the Laṅkā and Malaya mountains.
t.5.66.28: Soon you will see Rāghava, the subduer of foes, his dwelling in the forest ended, consecrated as king in Ayodhyā together with you.
t.5.66.29: Then, soothed by me with kind and welcome words, the daughter of the Maithila king, whose speech was free of despondency, found peace through me, though she was so sorely afflicted by grief for you.
